title: Leading the Way: How GFiE Turns Experience Into Empowerment

content.content: Every journey brings unique insights, but for care-experienced individuals, turning lived experience into a career path can often feel like an uphill battle. That’s exactly where Going Forward into Employment (GFiE) steps in.

Aligned with this year’s ‘National Care Leavers Month’  theme, "Leading the Way: From Experience to Empowerment," GFiE is dedicated to unlocking potential, removing traditional hiring obstacles, and creating real opportunities for growth within public service.
Through a series of thoughtful initiatives, GFiE translates this theme into meaningful action and ensures every candidate is supported from application to career progression.
How GFiE Removes Barriers
Traditional job applications can feel overwhelming, GFiE breaks down these hurdles by focusing on potential rather than academic credentials or complex competency frameworks.

GFiE emphasises care-experienced individuals as self-determined leaders rather than passive recipients of care and acknowledges them as key advocates championing meaningful transformation throughout the care system.
Making It Happen

When GFiE received some roles in DWP, based in Leeds, we were keen to work with Leeds City Council's Employment and Skills team, who are delivering the newly formed Healthy Working Lives Skills and Employment (Connect to Work) service. Having spoken to the team, we knew that their remit involved providing up to 12 months of personalised, one-to-one support with an employment specialist. The programme focuses on:

Our experience of the service demonstrated the above - we were able to arrange a drop in session with some of the care-experienced young people to demystify the role and answer any questions. The team at Leeds City Council supported the young people to write applications that clearly outlined their transferable skills and strengths.
Going forward to interviews, the candidates described themselves as feeling at ease, and the vacancy holders were able to see their potential and alignment to DWP’s values.
Local partners working in this way led to successful offers for all of the roles, and we hope this will be just the start of some fantastic careers for the care-experienced young people.
Get Involved & Learn More

Whether you’re a care leaver ready to begin your career journey or a manager looking to host a placement, GFiE provides the guidance, network, and tools to help you succeed. Head over to the GFiE blog to explore candidate stories, access support resources, and find out how you can get involved today!

title: Five practical foundations for artificial intelligence (AI) readiness

content.content: Artificial intelligence (AI) is changing how teams across government work. AI tools can help people find information, analyse data, develop ideas and complete routine tasks. But using AI tools is only one part of being ready for AI. Government also needs strong digital and data foundations. Teams need to understand the technology they use and where data is held and processed. teams also need to know how new ideas can move safely from early testing into live services. The State of digital government review highlights the need to strengthen these foundations to take full advantage of AI. Here are 5 practical areas teams can focus on. 1. Map government's technology infrastructure Government's technology infrastructure has changed significantly over the past decade. The Government’s Cloud First policy, introduced in 2013, encouraged public sector organisations to consider public cloud services before other options. Cloud services now support many government tools and services, bringing greater flexibility and access to new technologies. However, teams also need a clear view of how their systems, technologies and suppliers connect. This can help them understand how existing cloud solutions could work alongside newer approaches. These include WebGPU, which processes data directly on a user's device, and on-premises hosting, such as edge computing, where data is processed close to where it is collected. A clearer picture of government's technology infrastructure can help teams make informed choices about AI, identify risks earlier and spot opportunities to share and reuse technology. The Cloud Challenge Book 2026 explores this challenge. It invites industry to work with government on issues including legacy modernisation and the digital infrastructure needed for an AI era. 2. Understand where data is processed Being ready for AI means understanding what happens to the data that feeds AI models. Teams should know:

Technologists need enough understanding to make informed decisions and manage risk effectively. The GOV.UK principles for securing personal data in government services highlight the importance of knowing who owns data and who is accountable for its security. The AI Playbook for Government provides practical guidance on using AI safely, responsibly and effectively. Addressing these questions early helps teams identify and manage potential barriers before they become problems. Teams should also be open about how and where they have used AI in developing a tool, product or service. 3. Create a clear route from prototype to service A successful prototype is not the same as a live government service. AI tools can make it easier to test ideas and develop early versions of products. But teams still need a route into secure, reliable and supported services. Teams need to consider security, data protection, infrastructure, accessibility, ownership, approvals and ongoing support. The Technology Code of Practice and Service Standard help teams address these areas throughout development, rather than after a prototype is complete. Clear routes to live service can help teams identify requirements and decision makers earlier. This reduces delays when successful prototypes move towards production. The aim is not to create one platform or process for every project. It is to give data engineering teams a clearer route for building, testing and launching technology responsibly. 4. Build technology that can be reused and adapted Government already has strong examples of technology built once and made available to others. Services such as GOV.UK Pay, GOV.UK Notify and GOV.UK One Login help organisations meet common needs without building everything from scratch. Similar thinking can be applied to data and AI. Using open standards, clearly documented interfaces and reusable patterns can reduce duplication and help teams build on work that has already been tested. Reuse does not mean every team must use the same technology. It means helping people find what exists, assess whether it meets their needs and adapt it where appropriate. 5. Strengthen peer support AI readiness is about people as well as technology. Teams across government are working through similar questions about AI, data, cloud infrastructure, security and moving ideas into live services. Peer networks, such as the AI Community, can help people share what they have learned, find examples that have worked elsewhere and get support with common challenges. This is particularly valuable for smaller teams and organisations without extensive specialist resources. As AI develops, stronger connections between practitioners can help good practice spread more quickly and reduce duplicated effort. Building stronger foundations for AI Moving from AI adoption to safe, scalable AI enablement means looking beyond individual tools. By understanding our technology infrastructure and data, creating clearer routes from prototype to service, building reusable technology and strengthening peer support, we can create the foundations needed to use AI responsibly, securely and at scale. A practical place to start is with the data you already use. Read the guidance on making government datasets ready for AI and consider how you can make your data easier to find, understand, use and trust. You can also explore GDS guidance and resources on using AI safely, effectively and securely across government and the public sector. If you use data in algorithmic tools or AI that informs decisions with a public effect, or that interacts directly with the public, you may also need to publish an Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard (ATRS) record. Taking these steps early can help teams move from experimentation to AI services that are secure, sustainable and ready to scale.

description: Is government ready for AI? Five practical considerations can help teams understand their data, systems and infrastructure before adopting AI.

title: Update on the CMA's private dentistry market study

content.content: Millions of people across the UK rely on private dentistry. Around 60% of patients pay privately for at least some dental care. For many people, including those on low incomes and receiving state benefits, private care can be a necessity rather than a preference: it is their only route to essential treatment when NHS care is unavailable. Those unable to access NHS care or afford private treatment may delay care or go without altogether.

Thousands of dedicated dental professionals across the UK work hard to deliver dental care every day. Since millions of people rely on private dental provision for essential care, it is critical that the market is working well to deliver fair and affordable outcomes. This is why, in March 2026, the CMA launched a market study into private dental services.
What we've found so far

Private provision of an essential service can work well where effective competition rewards providers for offering better prices, quality, service and choice. Our emerging findings show that the private dental services market is not consistently working well for patients.
The problems we see are systemic:

Throughout our work it has become increasingly clear that public and private dentistry are deeply interconnected, often sharing the same practices and workforce. Government decisions on NHS funding, commissioning, contracts and workforce therefore shape not only patients’ choices about use of private care, but also providers’ incentives and behaviour and outcomes across the sector.

Our assessment of the evidence points to a market where patients often cannot exert the competitive pressure that would normally discipline prices and commercial behaviour. Dental care is a credence service: patients rely heavily on their dentist’s advice and cannot readily assess whether treatment is necessary, appropriate, good quality or good value, even after it is provided. Their ability and willingness to shop around is further constrained by their needs and preferences, including the importance of NHS availability, proximity and continuity of care or the need for urgent treatment. The information that is available on prices and treatment is often incomplete and difficult to compare. As a result, switching between practices is low and the competitive pressure exerted by patients is weak. Where patients do switch, the most common reason is moving home or workplace rather than seeking better value.
Shortage of dentists

Workforce constraints further weaken competition. The UK had 6.7 dentists per 10,000 people in 2024, compared with 8 or more in most European Economic Area countries. Recruitment and retention difficulties limit practices’ ability to expand and new providers’ ability to enter. Practices operating near capacity have little incentive to lower prices to attract more patients, while patients have fewer alternatives. Price competition is weak, despite a fragmented market in which independent firms account for over 60% of practices. We found examples of documents from among the four largest dental groups that focus on raising prices towards those of nearby practices rather than undercutting them. Some also refer to opportunities to increase prices due to patients’ limited price sensitivity, as well as to increase prices following acquisitions.
Commercial incentives

At the same time, practices and clinicians have commercial incentives to increase revenue. Dentists’ pay typically takes the form of a substantial share of the revenue generated by the treatment they provide, and owner-dentists benefit from practice profits and value. Internal documents from large groups show strategies to increase prices, convert NHS patients to private care, sell higher-value treatments and dental payment plans, and increase treatment and recall activity. Commercial incentives to increase profits are part and parcel of a private market and when combined with strong competition which rewards providers for offering better quality and prices, can be aligned with customer interests. But in private dentistry, patients’ reliance on professional advice and workforce constraints create a risk that commercial incentives to increase revenue may conflict with patients’ interests in obtaining good value dental care.

The outcomes we observe are consistent with that diagnosis. Prices at large dental groups increased by an estimated 7% a year on average between 2023 and 2025, ahead of consumer price inflation and wage growth. We have also seen significant variation in prices in local areas, for example, listed minimum prices for a composite white filling ranged from £80 to £223 in Preston. But patients are not easily able to find and switch to potentially better-value options.

In addition, we have identified variation in outcomes across the regions and nations of the UK, for example in terms of access to dental services, affordability and workforce capacity. This means that where a patient lives can affect both what care is available and what it costs relative to income.
Gaps in regulation

Regulation provides important consumer protections, but it is both complex and not as effective as it could be. It focuses heavily on individual professionals, even where many decisions that impact patients are taken by practice owners, managers or groups. Enforcement is often geared towards the most serious professional misconduct, complaints and redress routes are difficult to navigate, and relevant NHS or consumer protections do not always appear to be enforced. Providers also report complexity, duplication and administrative burden. In our emerging view, the answer is therefore not more regulation but better-focused accountability, proportionate enforcement and accessible redress.
What we're proposing

Our emerging view is that a substantial package of interconnected changes is required to deliver better outcomes in this market. Our proposals aim to create the conditions in which dental professionals and businesses can thrive by meeting patients’ needs well, while widening access to affordable essential care. The issues we have found are systemic, rather than a judgement on individual dental professionals.
We provisionally propose a mutually reinforcing package of measures which would:

Measures to improve information, comparison and switching, increase workforce capacity, and reform regulation and redress should together deliver substantial improvements for patients. These reforms are necessary, but not in our view sufficient on their own to address the systemic issues in this market. Patients cannot be expected to transform this essential market simply by voting with their feet, and regulation cannot substitute fully for effective competitive constraints. Rather, governments will need to intervene further, playing a more direct market-shaping role, and using their position as major purchasers and commissioners of dentistry to influence incentives and outcomes for private as well as NHS patients. Failing this, price controls might be needed to ensure good outcomes.
Next steps

These are interim findings and proposals and we invite further input and insight from across the sector. During the next phase of the study we will consult on our analysis, deepen our evidence on prices, profitability, ownership, financing and local outcomes, and work with stakeholders to understand how real change could be achieved in this critically important market.

Our final recommendations will aim to take into account policy and practical differences between nations and regions, as well as the importance of preserving clinical judgement, workforce supply, and provider viability. In assessing their feasibility and likely impact, we will take account not only of the market as it stands today but consider how different market dynamics arising from a package of measures might combine to change incentives and outcomes over time.
We want to hear from you
We're consulting on our interim report and findings.
Share your views by 17 December.
We'll publish our final report by the statutory deadline of 4 March 2027.

title: We’re introducing a new way for customers to register with us

content.content: We’re introducing a new online service, making it easier for people who need a Customer Reference Number (CRN) to register and access the Rural Payments service.   This change will make registering with us more convenient by allowing customers to self-serve, while strengthening identity checks.  A CRN is the unique number used to identify customers who use our services. New customers who need to request a CRN could include:
If you already have a CRN, you don’t need to register again.
A new self-serve process
To request a CRN, a new customer will:
Using GOV.UK One Login
GOV.UK One Login provides a secure way to sign in and prove your identity when using government services.

Because GOV.UK One Login is linked to the individual, you must complete your own identity verification. An agent can’t do this on your behalf.  If an agent doesn’t already have their own CRN, they’ll also need to complete the new registration process using their own GOV.UK One Login. The appropriate permissions will still need to be in place on the Rural Payments service before an agent can act for a customer or business.
Support will still be available
We understand that some customers will need help with the new service.
An offline route will remain available for customers who cannot complete the online process. More information about this support will be provided before the new service is introduced.
What happens next
The new registration service is currently planned for December 2026. We’ll share more information before it’s introduced so customers and agents know what to expect and where to go for help.
Existing customers do not need to do anything. If you already have a CRN, you should continue to use it as normal.

title: From coral reefs to farming communities: measuring the impact of Defra’s international work

content.content: Climate change, nature loss and pollution do not stop at national borders.

When ecosystems break down, food, water, health and economies unravel – fuelling poverty, instability, insecurity and conflict across the globe. This is particularly critical in developing countries, where much of the world’s biodiversity is concentrated.

Defra’s international programmes are delivered across a range of developing countries. They focus on critical global ecosystems that underpin UK resilience and national security and where the potential for impact on poverty and biodiversity outcomes is greatest.
Understanding the impact of our international investments is crucial in helping us to target funding where it will make the most difference.
Today we have published our 2026 annual results, our latest estimate of what we’ve achieved through Defra’s international programmes.
The figures show that, through Defra-supported programmes:
But the numbers only tell part of the story. For me, the important question is: what is changing for the people whose lives and livelihoods depend on nature?

Behind the numbers are communities changing how natural resources are managed, farmers adopting safer and more sustainable approaches, and partnerships helping protect ecosystems on which people depend.
Protecting oceans and livelihoods

The scale of this work is particularly visible in the Coral Triangle in South-East Asia. Coral reefs support food security, climate resilience and livelihoods, but are threatened by overfishing and habitat destruction.

Across Indonesia and the Philippines, seven Defra-supported marine programmes have directly enabled sustainable management of an estimated 1.08 million hectares of marine, coastal and mangrove environments – an area roughly half the size of Wales.

One example is a sustainable fisheries project in Southeast Sulawesi, Indonesia, supported through the Ocean Risk and Resilience Action Alliance. It is working with local communities to protect important reefs and breeding areas while maintaining sustainable fishing and livelihoods.

So far, three locally managed areas have been established, putting around 22,000 hectares under community-led sustainable fisheries management. Hundreds of coastal community representatives have helped map and design the areas and make decisions about how they should be managed. Some sites are already showing stable or increasing fish populations, reduced destructive fishing and community patrols to protect no-take zones.
Supporting farmers to make lasting change
Our results are also about people and the connection between a healthy environment and secure livelihoods.

In Vietnam, Defra’s Environmental Pollution Programme has supported farmers to adopt integrated pest management, an approach that uses better understanding of crops and natural pest-control methods to reduce reliance on chemical pesticides. The initiative trained more than 6,500 farmers to limit their chemical pesticide use.
On participating tea farms, insecticide use fell by 82% within two years. Farmers adopting the approach recorded annual incomes 10% to 31% higher than conventional farmers.

Importantly, the project was designed to ensure that its benefits are shared equitably rather than concentrated among the majority. This has included establishing 32 female-led farmer groups and 21 demonstration farms managed by women.
For me, examples like these are an important reminder of why measuring results and capturing stories matters. It helps us understand what is changing, who benefits and where we can improve.
Being open about what the numbers tell us
Caring about the people behind the results also means being honest about the evidence.

These results are estimates. Programmes and partners work in very different settings, and their data can vary in completeness and accuracy. Before publication, Defra analysts review the information and supporting evidence, making adjustments where necessary to avoid overstating our impact.
I want readers to understand both what the figures show and their limits. A large number is not the whole story, and it should not stand in for evidence about what is changing for people and nature.

That is why reporting matters. It connects the bigger picture with changes in people’s lives and helps us understand how protecting nature around the world contributes to a more secure future, abroad and at home.
Read the report in full.

title: Natural England and Department for Work and Pensions: a partnership for people, skills and nature

content.content: Author: David Drake, Director of People and Nature at Natural England.

Natural England and the Department for Work and Pensions have launched a new partnership to help young people overcome barriers to employment through nature-based activities, skills development and improved wellbeing. The initiative will create pathways into volunteering, training and green jobs while supporting nature recovery across England. The partnership aims to help more young people access meaningful work while developing the skilled workforce needed to restore and protect nature across England.

Thousands of young people face barriers to employment, often linked to confidence, wellbeing and limited opportunities to gain practical experience. At the same time, evidence continues to show that spending time in nature can improve wellbeing, build skills and strengthen connections with communities.

That's why Natural England and the Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) have launched a new partnership to help more people build skills, improve wellbeing and move towards employment while contributing to nature recovery across England.

The partnership brings together Natural England's expertise in nature recovery and connecting people with nature, alongside DWP's reach into communities across the country. Together, we will create opportunities that help people access training, volunteering and employment while contributing to nature recovery.

Research continues to demonstrate the benefits of spending time in nature. The People and Nature Survey found that 89% of regular visitors felt that nature benefited their mental health and wellbeing. However, access to nature remains unequal, with people in poorer health and those living in more deprived communities less likely to spend time outdoors.

The partnership supports the ambitions set out in the recently published Milburn Review, which highlighted the need for earlier support and better integration of health and employment services for young people.
Supporting young people through nature
One of the first initiatives under the partnership is a pilot programme in the North East of England for young people who are not in education, employment or training (NEETs).

Starting this month, young people referred through local Jobcentres and Youth Hubs will take part in a six-week programme of nature-based activities designed to improve wellbeing, develop practical skills and support progression into volunteering, training or work.

In Sunderland, activities will be delivered in partnership with Durham Wildlife Trust at Rainton Meadows Nature Reserve, where participants will gain hands-on experience in habitat management and countryside skills.
The pilot builds on learning from previous programmes that demonstrated the value of nature-based activities in developing transferable skills and supporting people facing barriers to employment.
Supporting green skills, jobs and nature recovery

A key focus of the partnership is helping people access opportunities within the growing green economy. Natural England and DWP will work together to connect people with skills development, work experience and employment opportunities, while helping to build the workforce needed to deliver nature recovery across England.

This work complements the Government's Youth Guarantee, which is expanding access to training, employment and workplace opportunities for young people. As demand for skills in nature recovery, conservation and environmental management continues to grow, nature-based programmes can help create pathways into rewarding careers while supporting economic growth and environmental improvement.

The expansion of the Jobs Guarantee creates further opportunities to connect young people with practical experience and meaningful work. Through this partnership, Natural England and DWP will explore how opportunities across the nature and conservation sector can support young people to gain experience, develop employability skills and take their next step towards long-term employment.

Nature recovery is one of the country's biggest long-term challenges, requiring a skilled and diverse workforce. By helping more people develop the skills and experience needed to work in environmental roles, this partnership can contribute to both thriving communities and a healthier natural environment.
Creating joined-up support through Youth Hubs and communities

Alongside this, Natural England and DWP are exploring opportunities to enhance nature within and around Jobcentres and Youth Hubs. Access to green spaces can create more positive environments for staff and service users and encourage engagement with employment services.

This aligns with the Milburn Review's vision for bringing employment, skills, health and wider support together locally. It also supports wider ambitions to create more green space in towns and cities, delivering benefits for physical and mental health, community cohesion and access to nature for people who may not otherwise experience it.
Working together for people and nature

Through this partnership, Natural England and DWP will help more people access the benefits of nature while creating pathways into training and employment. By investing in both people and places, we can create opportunities for individuals, strengthen local communities and help ensure that nature's recovery benefits everyone, now and for generations to come.

title: MHRA expectations concerning packaging operations to minimise the risk of mix-ups

content.content: Problems during packaging operations involving the mix-up of components and products present an unacceptable risk to patient safety. There have recently been a number of recalls initiated, and several critical deficiencies raised by GMP Inspectors, due to failures to implement adequate controls during packaging operations.

This blog is intended to draw attention to the risks associated with packaging operations and outline the expectations of the MHRA that will be reviewed during inspections. The principles should be extended to other areas where mix-ups may occur. For example, it has been known for companies to mix up granules prior to compression into tablets and filling into hard shell capsules.
Risk Assessment, Identification and Control

One of the foundations of Good Manufacturing Practice (GMP) is the appropriate implementation of Quality Risk Management (QRM) principles. This is described in ICH Q9 and EU GMP Chapter 1 as the design of the system should incorporate appropriate risk management principles including the use of appropriate tools. GMP is explicit in Chapter 1.3 that QRM tools should be used to review critical processes, identify specific risk factors, and ensure robust controls are in place.

Well-controlled primary and secondary packaging operations are critical to the safety, quality and efficacy of medicinal products. Therefore, sufficiently detailed risk assessments should be performed to identify potential hazards and the controls necessary to protect patient safety. These assessments should confirm that controls are in place and effective or generate actions (CAPAs) to implement additional controls where required.

Generic risk assessments that are high-level and confirmatory in nature, for example simply confirming that general procedures are in place, are unlikely to be of sufficient substance to protect patient safety and demonstrate compliance with GMP.
Component Version Control
Version control of documentation within the Pharmaceutical Quality System is a given. Universally, controlled documents are allocated unique reference numbers and version numbers.

However, despite printed packaging components stating legally required information that is often critical to those prescribing, dispensing and taking medicines, there are occasions when companies do not version-control printed packaging component specifications and/or artwork master documents or indeed the printed items themselves using unique item codes.
This is poor practice, as it is essential that only the current approved version of any packaging item is used in production.

The sole use of internal batch numbers or GRNs for picking and checking packaging materials onto the line without reference to the material itself is not an adequate mechanism to provide proper control.
Line Clearance

Suitable line clearance is a specific requirement of EU GMP Chapter 5. However, poor application of QRM principles often leads to underdeveloped Standard Operating Procedures and Work Instructions that lack detail and clear roles and responsibilities.
Subject matter experts should be involved in designing an appropriate process with a clear appreciation of where product and component entrapment within machines is possible.

Attention should also be paid to ancillary equipment such as de-blistering machines, product and packaging rejection points, and computerised systems where variable print data can be retained and carried over.
Adequate time should be allowed for line clearance, as it is easy for areas to be overlooked by busy staff endeavouring to change over the line to meet scheduling demands.
Consideration should be given to dedicating personnel to the checking of completed line clearance where they can operate free from distraction and competing priorities.

Additional controls and checks may be required where changeover processes permit packaging materials to be retained on the line and carried over from one batch to another, particularly where there are changes in product strength during campaign packaging.

Once line-clearance processes are designed, there must be adequate means to ensure that knowledge is translated into consistent and reliable action by staff. A comprehensive training process is expected, with consideration given to practical assessments and challenge exercises. Companies should ensure that any checklists are supported by appropriately comprehensive procedures and/or reference guides, and that high-risk entrapment locations are clearly understood and identifiable so that misinterpretation of requirements is minimised to the greatest extent possible.
Technology

Pharmacode technology has been available for approximately 50 years; however, not all automated commercial packaging operations have this installed on their equipment or available within their artwork. Equally, other types of printed packaging materials do not routinely have corresponding online technology to verify the identity of what has been provided for packaging operations, for example lidding foil.
Regulation 74(1) of the Human Medicines Regulations 2012 (SI 2012/1916) states:

"The holder of a UK marketing authorisation must keep under review the methods of manufacture and control of the product to which the authorisation relates, taking account of scientific and technical progress."

Marketing Authorisation Holders and manufacturers should endeavour to ensure that, where technological controls are available, these are utilised, particularly where the consequence of error could cause significant harm to patients.

Where technological controls are not available, suitable organisational controls must be implemented in line with QRM principles. These controls cannot be static and should be reviewed regularly in line with equipment functionality and site operations. For example, where pharmacode readers are installed and a breakdown occurs, detectability of a mix-up risk will be reduced. The QRM process should identify this and balance the risk by implementing other mitigations to ensure that mix-up risks are not inappropriately elevated in the short term.
Reconciliation of Packaging Components

The objective of undertaking reconciliation of materials following packaging operations is not simply to ensure that a figure of 100% can be recorded in the batch record. It is to identify potential mix-ups, or other failures within the process (for example, missing product or patient information leaflets), through careful evaluation to confirm that operations have been completed properly and without error.

Perfect reconciliation figures can, on a superficial level, be attractive targets. However, for large-scale packaging operations, these may be unrealistic and can lead to poor behaviours, such as "finding extra waste", in order to avoid investigations and delays to line changeovers.

QRM principles should be used to establish reconciliation limits (inclusive of bulk) based on the risks associated with the process and product, such as batch size, product potency, toxicity, and intended use or patient population.

Inherent variability in component quantities supplied by approved vendors should be understood. Outputs from the QRM process can be used as inputs into vendor-assurance programmes and Quality Technical Agreements, so that suitable upstream controls and limits are implemented to provide maximum assurance that reconciliation activities remain reliable indicators.

In addition, label reconciliation can be hampered where labels on a reel are not sequentially numbered, making it difficult to establish an accurate quantity. Internal QC sampling operations should be carefully controlled to ensure that any quantity changes are documented and visible to production staff.
It must also be understood that yield and reconciliation are different concepts. Regrettably, this continues to be misunderstood.
Storage

Earlier in this article, I described how not all components are routinely printed with pharmacodes and gave lidding foil as an example. Surprisingly, it remains common to find reels of lidding foil for different products, or more alarmingly, for the same product but a different strength, stored together in the same location, sometimes on the same or adjacent pallet or rack and without any physical segregation.

This approach has facilitated an error chain to develop that directly led to a Class 2 recall. Careful attention to process design using QRM principles should reasonably be expected to identify such practices and drive improvement.

During inspections, materials of different status have been found in staging areas adjacent to packaging lines. For example, materials that have been fully checked and released by QC/QA and are ready for packaging have been stored alongside materials awaiting release by QC/QA that have been transferred to the area for convenience without any clear differentiation between the two.
It is vitally important that the status of any stock can be readily ascertained and that adequate segregation is maintained, whether physical and/or electronic, to prevent mix-ups.
Customer Complaints

Customer complaints are an important mechanism for identifying product defects that have, despite a site's best efforts, escaped its controls. As such, customer complaints should be considered properly and with an open mind.

With particular consideration to packaging errors, routine reviews of batch records, deviations raised at the time, and inspection of retain samples are important. However, these activities, together with a justification that procedures are in place, are not sufficiently robust on their own to categorically rule out the possibility that a genuine complaint has been received.

Except where reported mix-ups involve products not manufactured at the same facility, careful evaluation of the circumstances and the potential for a mix-up during manufacture or within the supply chain (hospitals, pharmacies or the patient's home) is imperative.

This should include establishing the affected products and batches and identifying potential chronological and/or physical overlap within the manufacturing facility. For example, were the batches in the production area at the same time? Were they processed or packaged on adjacent lines?

Trending of customer complaints should be performed on an ongoing basis and used when considering the overall validity and extent of reported product defects so that appropriate risk-reducing actions can be taken.
Conclusion

When designing and undertaking packaging operations, EU GMP Chapter 5 requires particular attention to be given to minimising the risk of cross-contamination, mix-ups and substitutions. To do this effectively, the Pharmaceutical Quality System (PQS) should incorporate appropriate Quality Risk Management principles, including the use of suitable tools.

GMP Inspectors often hear from companies that failures could never occur because checks are performed at each stage of established processes. However, those Inspectors, as well as the MHRA Defective Medicines Report Centre (DMRC), regularly encounter situations where those "never events" have indeed occurred and, regrettably, continue to occur.
Complacency through a lack of critical review and continuous improvement of technologies and procedures is itself a significant risk to product quality.

Companies should use the examples described in this article to inspire their own critical review of their operations, rather than assume that these failures could not occur at their site. Qualified Persons should ensure that this review is undertaken and that they have properly considered the risks identified and the effectiveness of the controls in place as part of their ongoing assurance that production operations comply with GMP. The review should involve those who undertake and oversee the activities, with attention given to how controls operate in practice, not simply how they are described in procedures. Where weaknesses are identified, appropriate actions should be assigned, implemented in a timely manner and checked for effectiveness. It should not take a customer complaint, a product recall or an inspection finding to prompt this review.
Inspectors will verify that a robust approach has been taken to minimise these risks and, in doing so, ensure that public health is being properly safeguarded.

title: Out of the box: a reusable template for case management

content.content: How many times do government teams design and build a case management capability from scratch?

At the Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade (BIST), we have multiple services dedicated to case management, particularly for managing different types of trade licence applications. Case management services receive, review and progress applications from submission to decision.
Although these services may serve different policy areas, many solve similar problems. Case management services need similar things:
Building these common parts separately for every service can duplicate effort. It can also make services more expensive and complex to maintain.
Putting reuse to the test
What if we stopped designing and building case management services for each separate policy area in isolation?
What if, instead, we built a user-centred template based on shared capabilities and functionality that is ready to go – ‘out of the box’ –  when the next policy request comes in?

This is the question a keen group of reusable enthusiasts asked themselves during a recent Firebreak project. Our aim was to take one licensing case management service and test whether the same structure, design and code could be applied to a different licence and policy context, within a week.
We were not trying to build a finished product. We wanted to test our vision that designs and code can, and should, be replicated and iterated rather than recreated.

Speed was everything. We wanted to demonstrate what might be possible when we treat common case management needs as reusable capabilities at pace. Our bigger ambition is to turn our rough prototype into a longer-term reusable foundation.
The problem, and indeed the solution, is not a new one. A cross-government working group has also explored an ‘applying for something’ service pattern, which is a relevant example for our project.
There has already been plenty of excellent work done at BIST on licensing case management services and reusable design patterns. This means that we were not starting with this problem from scratch.
Designing for reuse

We started with evidence-backed patterns from an existing licensing service and reusable information flows based on existing user research insights and content design best practice. Our aim was to create a simple baseline that other services could build on.
That changed the question we were asking. Rather than, ‘what does this current service use?’, we asked, ‘which parts could another service use?’
That small shift changed how we approached the design.
For example, licence applications often ask users to add several things of the same type. These might be products, organisations, people or documents.
Instead of designing separate interactions for each one, we explored reusable patterns that allow users to add information, see a summary, then change, remove or add another item.
We also looked at how information entered earlier in an application could change what users are asked to do later.
For example, an answer could trigger a mandatory document upload. The service could then tell the user exactly what they need to provide, rather than expecting them to remember.
These are relatively simple ideas on their own. The interesting part is thinking about them as building blocks that can be combined in different ways.
What we built in 5 days
By the end of Firebreak, we had created a prototype licensing service using reusable capabilities.
It allowed external users to:
It also allowed internal users to:

Rather than just producing individual screens, we had enough of the end-to-end journey to demonstrate how reusable design and technical capabilities could work together, particularly when capturing structured data.
The prototype does not prove that we now have a reusable case management product ready for every situation. We do not.

What it does give us is something tangible. Instead of discussing reuse as an abstract ambition, we have demonstrated that reusing existing code and designs allows us to build at pace to test a prototype properly. It is then possible to customise, based on specific service needs at a fraction of the design and build time usually required.
Watch members of the Firebreak project team Cal Gott (Senior Business Analyst) and Karwai Pun (Lead Interaction Designer) discuss and give a demo of what we managed to achieve in 5 days.
If you would like a full demo of our prototype, you can contact us through the comments.
Where could this go next?
We hope to take what we built during Firebreak and apply that to real-world licensing examples.
First, we want to develop the prototype into a workable end-to-end licensing service and identify which parts form a genuinely reusable core.

The real test would then come with a second licensing journey. How quickly could we adapt what already exists? Which parts would transfer cleanly, and which would need to change? Crucially, we would measure how much time the reusable approach saves.
The project would be as much a discovery as it would be a delivery opportunity. There will be new questions and challenges as we go.
We also plan to add any patterns, components and capabilities we create as part of this work to BIST’s wider design system, so other teams can build on them too.
What we learned

Our biggest lesson was how much value already exists in previous work. That includes not only designs and code, but the research and insight that led to them. Before creating something new, it is worth asking whether another team has already solved part of the problem.
Reusable design and code are not only valuable, but vital in a landscape that demands more from digital teams, with increasingly less time and fewer resources.
That does not mean every government service should look or work in exactly the same way. It means recognising where our problems overlap and treating that overlap as an opportunity.
Firebreak was also a great opportunity to turn the regular constraint of time into a fun challenge between colleagues – to see what we can create when we’re on the clock.

Five focused days will not solve every problem. But opportunities like this can give a multidisciplinary team enough space to challenge assumptions, make an idea tangible and show what might be possible. What do you think you could achieve in 5 days?

title: Could your school recover money from its energy bills?

content.content: We can check if your school is paying the right price for gas and electricity. We look back up to six years.

We know that managing energy contracts is complex. That's why the Department for Education (DfE) used a Government Commercial Agency (GCA) framework to appoint a company called PCMG. It checks your gas and electricity bills for errors and helps you claim back any money you're owed.

This is not just for schools who think they've been overcharged. It's also for schools who simply want peace of mind that their bills are correct. There's no upfront cost, and PCMG only charges a fee if it recovers money or finds savings.
This contract has recently been extended to include colleges and Further Education (FE) establishments to ensure the education sector can fully benefit from the service.
Why this matters to you

Energy bills are complicated, and mistakes happen more often than you'd think. Even if nothing seems wrong, a specialist check can confirm you're paying the right amount or uncover savings you didn't know were there.
PCMG reviews your billing history going back up to six years. It looks for billing errors, missed refunds or credits, incorrect charges, and potential ongoing savings.
The aim is simple. We want to help you find any money owed back to your school, or savings you can make going forward.
One school recovered over £26,000

Cressex Community School in High Wycombe has 765 pupils and electricity bills of over £200,000 a year. School Business Manager Vicki Hillier always tried to check her bills were correct but found it nearly impossible to be sure.
"You're never quite sure if those charges are all at the right rates," she said. "You do your best to find out, but you don't always know who to ask."
Because the service is DfE-approved, Vicki felt confident it was trustworthy. She submitted her school's historical bills, and within months received a detailed report.

The audit found errors worth over £26,000. This included £6,047 refunded from incorrect climate change levy charges and £20,063 in VAT charged at the wrong rate. It also identified potential ongoing savings of £720 a month.

"Having expert advice gave us the reassurance to act," Vicki said. Asked if she'd recommend the service, she said, "Yes, definitely. It's straightforward, it's worth doing, and it's a transparent process."
Questions schools often ask us
We've heard from schools who are put off using this service because they think it will create extra work, or because they're not sure who does what. Let's clear up some concerns:
"Will this create a lot of work for my team?"  Not much. Your main job is to send some paperwork and your bills to PCMG. After that, PCMG does the hard work of checking, negotiating, and chasing.
"Is this only for schools with a problem?" No. Many schools use this service simply to confirm they are paying the correct amount. Think of it as a free health check for your energy contract.

"Do I need to be an energy expert to use this service?"  No. PCMG's specialists understand energy contracts and billing in detail, so you do not need to know anything about tariffs or supplier jargon.

"Will PCMG make decisions about my energy contract without me?" No. PCMG can only speak to your energy supplier once you give them written approval. No recommendations or recoveries are actioned without your say. You stay in control throughout.
What you'll get
There's no upfront cost. If PCMG does not find anything, you pay nothing. If they do, their fee is 18% of whatever they recover or save you, under the terms of the DfE framework.
How the process works
How to get started
You can access the service by applying through the energy cost recovery services for schools page on GOV.UK
When you have done this, you will complete the Letter of Engagement that will allow access to the DfE contract.
This is followed by a Letter of Authority, that will allow PCMG to speak to your energy supplier.
Ready to check your energy bills?
Whether you think something's wrong, or you just want peace of mind, now's a good time to get your bills checked.
Apply today via GOV.UK Get Help Buying for Schools.

Any savings, benefits and outcomes described in this blog were provided by Cressex Community School and reflect its specific experience and circumstances. Individual results will vary between schools and trusts.

title: How dedicated funding for books and reading materials helped our students choose their next chapter

content.content: It’s always exciting choosing a new book – Jenny Webb, Trust Director of English and Literacy at Carlton Academy Trust, tells us how she got students involved in deciding which books to buy with money from Department for Education.
An opportunity to bring new books into our schools
We were so delighted to find out that, as part of the National Year of Reading, our school had been allocated dedicated DfE funding for books – ring-fenced money for us to make the most of!
The magic of a real book

There's something profound and magical about holding a book. When you think about it, the physical reality of books is almost surreal: ultra-thin slices of bleached tree pulp, bound into volumes, inscribed with tiny symbols.

But these strange and ingenious objects enable us to carry entire worlds around with us. They hold vast quantities of information, epic tales, journeys and transformations, all in a thing which is small, light and easy to navigate. It’s remarkable, really.
From learning to read, to choosing to read

Reading is central to our work at Carlton Academy Trust and, while our number one priority is ensuring that children can read, the imperative to encourage and empower them to choose to read comes in as a close second.
We want our young people to exist in the presence of real books and feel that thrilling, stimulating, therapeutic magic.
Bringing books within everyone’s reach
Many of the children across our secondary schools in West Yorkshire don't have books in their own homes.

In our opinion, a school isn’t a school unless it's also a home of books. Our schools all have their own librarians and dedicated spaces for books, and we work hard to ensure that these are places where students’ voices and experiences are known and valued.
So, how did we decide how to spend the money?
We asked the children, of course.
All our schools approached this with the same principles, but in ways which suited their unique cohorts. The processes were led in each case by our fabulous librarians.
1.) Surveying students about what they would like to see in the library
In some schools, we held in-person conversations and panels. In others, this was an initial paper or digital questionnaire. We asked students to tell us:
2.) Forming groups to come together and make choices
We brought together groups of students to help make choices, either drawing on a broad range of voices or focusing on cohorts of students we wanted to see in the library more.

For instance, we spoke to a target group of year 9 boys who don’t currently read by choice. We also had a focus group of girls with SEND, and a group of new year 7 students. They all had really interesting perspectives and helped us to shape our thinking.
3.) Making a final selection
We took many things into consideration but were mostly directed by the choices of the students themselves. In addition, we considered:
4.) Planning to share books with students
When our books arrive, we plan to have launch events to make sure students know about all the new options and can see how their ideas and requests have become reality.
In some schools, there's a plan to have dedicated ‘private’ launches for small groups of students who may benefit from exploring these new texts in a calmer, more peaceful environment.
We can’t wait to receive the books and see what our students choose to read.

All state-funded secondary schools in England are eligible for this funding, which can also be used for other reading materials including e-books and audiobooks. For more information, see the DfE guidance here.

title: Windermere's water quality: what the latest classifications tell us

content.content: Elizabeth Maerz and Josh Barton

Water quality in Windermere has been the subject of considerable public attention.  The Water Framework Directive is one way in which water quality is measured. But what do these classifications measure, and what do the latest results tell us about the health of Windermere and the wider catchment?   In this blog, we break down how the classification system works, what the results reveal about progress being made, and where there's more work to be done.  Whether you're new to the topic or already following the data closely, we hope this is a clear guide to understanding what's really happening beneath the surface.
What are Water Framework classifications?

Water Framework classifications are the way the Environment Agency is legally required to check the health of our rivers and lakes in England. The goal is simple: stop them getting worse, protect the wildlife that lives in them, and help them become healthier and more natural over time.

Every water body in England is classified as: High, Good, Moderate, Poor or Bad. High means it's in near-natural condition. Good means there's only slight disturbance from human activity. Poor means the ecosystem is heavily damaged and Bad means the water environment is severely degraded. The target is for every water body is to reach at least Good.
The latest results came out on 31 July 2026, these were based on three years of monitoring, giving us a picture of how water quality is changing over time.
How the scoring works
Each water body gets an overall score made up of two parts.

Chemical status checks priority Substances and Priority Hazardous Substances (such as specific synthetic pollutants, heavy metals, and pesticides) that pose significant risks to the water environment or human health. It can be either GOOD or FAIL as there are very strict standards for these specific chemical substances.

Ecological status looks at the wildlife (fish, plants, algae) and physico-chemical elements which act as supporting conditions that help sustain wildlife in water. These include oxygen levels, pH (acidity/alkalinity), temperature and nutrients (nitrogen and phosphorus). Nitrogen and phosphorus are essential for life, but too much of either, or the wrong form, can cause pollution. Ecological elements are rated High, Good, Moderate, Poor or Bad.

No waterbody in the Windermere catchment achieved Good Overall Status. This is due to the chemical status failing. This is not unique to Windermere. Across England, all water bodies currently fail the national chemical status classification because of trace amounts of long-lasting pollutants, such as mercury and polybrominated diphenyl ethers (PBDEs) — chemicals previously used to make products such as furniture and electronics more fire-resistant.

Some harmful chemicals, such as mercury and PBDEs, can build up in animals and pass along the food chain. To help protect wildlife and people, we measure the levels of these chemicals in fish, crayfish and mussels and compare them with agreed safety limits. We do this at a small number of monitoring sites in the rivers that feed the lake, but not on Windermere itself.

The Environment Agency uses results from the locations it monitors to represent much larger geographical areas for classification purposes. This approach recognises that these substances are widespread in the environment and are found far beyond their original sources. Chemical status failures are common nationally (and across Europe) and are not unique to Windermere.
How do the water classification rules work?

One of the critical rules often referred to as the “one out, all out” rule.  The lowest-scoring biological element determines the Overall and Ecological status. Biological elements include things such as fish, aquatic plants (macrophytes), microscopic algae (phytoplankton) and invertebrates. These are considered the best indicators of the long-term health of a water body because their abundance and diversity reflect the conditions they have been living in over time.

Physical-chemical elements, such as phosphorus, dissolved oxygen, temperature and pH, support the biological classification and help us understand the pressures affecting a water body. If one of these supporting elements falls below Good, it can prevent a water body from achieving Good ecological status. However, only biological elements can drive the Overall and Ecological status below Moderate.
Think of it like a health check. The biology tells us how healthy the lake actually is, while the physical and chemical measurements help us understand what factors may be affecting it.

Windermere North Basin provides a good example of how this works. Although many of the elements assessed achieved Good or High status, nutrients like total phosphorus and total nitrogen, aquatic plants were classified as Moderate. As ecological status is driven by the lowest-scoring biological element, the overall ecological classification is also Moderate.

Grasmere provides another useful example. Dissolved oxygen is classified as Bad, which tells us there is a water quality issue that needs attention. However, the overall ecological status is Moderate because the lowest classified biological element, macrophytes, is classified as Moderate. This demonstrates how biological indicators determine ecological classification, while physical-chemical elements help explain the pressures acting on the water body
Where have there been water quality improvements in Windermere?
There's real progress to celebrate. Nutrient pollution, like phosphorus and nitrogen, is one of the biggest causes of algal blooms, and Windermere is improving on this front.

This didn't happen by accident. It's the result of years of work driving investment from the Water Company, United Utilities, changes in practices from farmers, landowners, businesses and local communities across the catchment.
Good news continues across the Windermere catchment: no lakes got worse. Grasmere improved to High for both phosphorus and algae. Elterwater reached High for phosphorus too.

Rivers tell a more mixed story. The Rothay and Leven both saw their temperature ratings slip to Good, and the Leven's fish rating dropped to Moderate. Cunsey Beck stayed at Poor, unchanged from last time, because of its fish population.
What's next
The phosphorus improvements show that investment and teamwork are paying off. But challenges like climate change and warmer water remain, so there's no room to be complacent.
These results also help us spot where to focus next. Esthwaite Water, for example, is showing several Moderate, Poor and Bad scores, suggesting it needs more concentrated attention.
The takeaway: improving water quality takes time, but progress in the Windermere catchment proves that sustained effort really does make a difference.

title: How Calverton Fish Farm Restocks England’s Rivers and Lakes

content.content: What does Calverton Fish Farm do?

Funded entirely by anglers’ fishing licence income, Calverton Fish Farm just outside Nottingham is a key part of the Environment Agency’s goal to maintain, develop and improve freshwater fisheries across the country.

We work with the Environment Agency’s 14 area fisheries teams to help determine what fish are needed and where. By closely working with angling clubs and fishery owners our area teams draw up a list of fish that are required each year. This can be for restocking after pollution incidents, on the back of habitat enhancement projects or to help create new fisheries. As a rule, we only stock where help is needed. We don’t stock hatchery fish where there are already healthy natural stocks present.
How Calverton rears fish for life in the wild

At Calverton, each season is busy, but autumn is exceptional, as this is the time when our fish are harvested from the large ‘growing on’ ponds on site, separated into their various species, sampled, counted and health-checked before they are ready for dispatch to a variety of rivers and lakes throughout England.

It takes approximately 18 months to rear our fish to a size where we can stock them out into rivers and lakes. All of the Calverton stocks are reared in semi-natural ponds that have lots of natural food, habitat, and plenty of flowing water. This ensures that our fish are fit enough to live in the rivers and that they can face the challenges that come from life in the wild.
Restocking the River Derwent in Derbyshire

One of these stockings took place on a cold and misty early November morning when on the banks of the River Derwent. We came to stock 1150 Chub, Dace, Roach and Barbel into the river, much to the excitement of the members of the local angling club in attendance.

We took the lids off the specially fitted tanks on the back of the pickup to reveal thousands of small shapes darting around in the bubbles of oxygenated water. A quick dip of the net and there was an explosion of silver and brown as hundreds of  Chub, Roach, Barbel and Dace got carried down to the river and released into the moving current.

It’s taken 18 months of hard work and painstaking processes to get the fish to this point; including a lot of work between the angling club and the local fisheries team. The best bit is seeing them swim off into their new home. It is so rewarding and makes all those early mornings, late nights and the hours of care and attention worthwhile.
How fishing licence income funds fish restocking

A similar stocking process will happen hundreds of times over the next couple of months at multiple sites as the team at the Fish Farm stock out over half a million coarse fish into England’s rivers and stillwaters.
It’s all made possible by anglers who buy their licences up and down the country. Without your investment, we could not carry out this vital work and so much more.
Find out more about buying a fishing licence and read more about our where your licence income goes in our annual report.

If you see illegal fishing activities on any inland water report in England, contact the Environment Agency’s Incident Hotline immediately on 0800 80 70 60 (available 24/7) or online via Report an Environmental Problem.

title: What do you get for your fishing licence fee?

content.content: By Richard Pitman, Calverton Fish Farm Manager and James Rabjohns, Fish Farm Technical Officer

When you buy a fishing licence, you're not only staying on the right side of the law, but you’re also helping the Environment Agency to support vital work that keeps England’s rivers, lakes and fisheries healthy and thriving.
But what is this ‘vital work’ that your hard-earned money helps support?

Fishing licence funding is invested back into fisheries. Last year this was more than £25 million, including over £1.2 million invested in over 250 fisheries improvement projects across England, directly benefiting more than 130,000 anglers with projects that directly improve fish stocks, habitats, angling access and facilities. The rest of the money funds our monitoring, enforcement, incident response and fish stocking.
We know from speaking with our licence holders there are a number of important issues which they want to see addressed and your fishing licence fee is key in helping achieve this.
Somewhere to fish
Having accessible and healthy fisheries is the bedrock of angling participation and we use fishing licence income to maintain, develop and improve places to fish.

Take the River Severn in Shrewsbury for example. We worked with Shrewsbury Town Fisheries who accessed our Fisheries Improvement Programme to get funds to install new, safe fishing platforms and improve access after the previous ones had degraded due to age and repeated flooding.
In total, we invested over £1.2 million of fishing licence income on over 250 fisheries improvement projects in 2025 to 2026, which:
All of which directly benefitted 132,378 anglers
Fish to catch
Whilst having places to fish is important, anglers are very keen to see healthy fish stocks in their fisheries.
Our fisheries officers work up and down the country work with angling clubs and fishing venues providing invaluable advice and guidance on how to run sustainable fisheries with good fish populations.

Sometimes though fisheries need an extra helping hand. Our Calverton Fish Farm, based in Nottinghamshire is a coarse fish hatchery which rears young fish to support lakes and rivers. When necessary, restocking helps boost fish populations and can be vital after environmental incidents or to kickstart the recovery of fisheries from long term issues, such as pollution.

One such fishery was Keynsham Angling Association’s Century Ponds in the south-west which we restocked with tench, crucian carp and roach after prolonged dry weather triggered an algal bloom which resulted in a fish kill.
Over the course of 2025 to 2026 Calverton stocked out 488,273 fish into rivers and stillwaters. All made possible by your fishing licence.
Fair play for those who pay

Fishing licence income allows us to carry out important fisheries enforcement work. Our dedicated band of Fisheries Enforcement Officers are out there 365 days a year upholding fisheries rules and regulations to ensure how our valuable fish stocks are protected.

In 2025 to 2026 our officers carried out over 50,000 licence checks to make sure people were fishing with a valid licence, ensuring that the evasion rate is very low. These checks help enforce the law whilst protecting our income to carry out other important fisheries work.

Licence checking though, is only one part of the job of our enforcement officers. They carry out a multitude of intelligence led roles which help protect our fisheries and the environment which you can see in this short video.
What you can do

So, what do you get for your licence fee? Probably a lot more than you imagined and all of which goes towards maintaining, improving and developing our freshwater fisheries for anglers and the public to enjoy.

If you see illegal fishing activities on any inland water report in England, contact the Environment Agency’s Incident Hotline immediately on 0800 80 70 60 (available 24/7) or use the official online Report an Environmental Problem tool.
You can read more about fishing licence funded fisheries work in our Fisheries Annual Report.

title: FiPL funding turns Dartmoor wool into rope for sea kelp farming
categories: Payments to support National Parks, National Landscapes and the Broads

content.content: Dartmoor National Park covers 954 square kilometres of wild, open moorlands, deep, wooded river valleys, and rare wildlife.

Historically sheep on Dartmoor were farmed for wool, in addition to meat. Many of Dartmoor's towns supported the wool trade. Dartmoor had local mills where shorn wool could be processed, providing jobs for local wool spinners and weavers.

During the 19th century, coal-powered mills off Dartmoor started to produce textiles faster and cheaper than Dartmoor's wool industry. Synthetic fibres also became popular, lowering demand for natural wool.

Whilst wool production has reduced, sheep farming and grazing remains active on Dartmoor. In recent years, the cost of shearing sheep and transporting fleece has for some farmers, exceeded the market price for raw wool.

That led Twool to find innovative new uses for wool. With Farming in Protected Landscapes (FiPL) funding, Twool have trialled using Dartmoor wool as a sustainable alternative to synthetic rope in sea kelp farming.
My name’s Bea, I’m a FiPL Adviser on Dartmoor and in this blog will talk you through the project’s journey.
FiPL: from moor to sea

Kelp farming is the cultivation of large brown seaweeds (like sugar kelp) in coastal ocean waters. Kelp is farmed on horizontal rope lines that are submerged below the water's surface. The ropes are secured with buoys which are attached to the rope and are then anchored to the seabed. Kelp uses sunlight and nutrients from the surrounding water to grow.
Kelp is used in agriculture as an alternative to fertiliser and to help manage drought, and as an ingredient in products from skincare to packaged foods.

Twool have been innovating in the wool industry since 2012, developing a wide range of new wool-based products over that time. They wanted to build on a successful Queen’s University Belfast trial and in 2024, Twool secured FiPL funding from the Dartmoor National Park Authority (DNPA) to  scale up production of rope for kelp farming, as a sustainable alternative to synthetic ropes.

At its heart, the project is collaborative, working closely with expert researchers at Queen's University Belfast, Twool as a local wool innovation business, and a number of Dartmoor farmers supplying their Whiteface Dartmoor sheep's wool. I’ll come on to talk more about collaboration in more detail.
Putting Dartmoor wool to the test
Whiteface Dartmoor sheep's wool is a strong, close lustrous wool with a durable curl/crimp and long staple length. This makes it ideal for spinning worsted (medium weight) yarn.
It’s long staple length means that this unique natural product can be braided easily into rope without getting stuck in modern milling machinery, unlike other types of sheep wool.

FiPL funded the processing, creation and deployment of 100m x 100m Dartmoor Whiteface wool rope lines used in Northern Ireland’s Strangford Lough in February 2024 as part of early proof of concept trials.
The rope was germinated with kelp seed ahead of deployment. Wool rope lines remained anchored down for six months and kelp grew well.
Strengthening a local wool supply chain
Creating a new market for Dartmoor wool requires more than developing an innovative product. It also requires the infrastructure to collect, process and store wool locally.

Since 2017, Greenwell Farm have been utilising an existing barn on site to store, pack and collect Dartmoor wool for members of the farming community, including Whiteface Dartmoor wool. Twool then buys this wool for its research trials into new uses for wool.
To the best of our knowledge, this is now the only location on Dartmoor that has the infrastructure to fully sort, press and pack wool locally.

Greenwell Farm applied separately for FiPL funding to purchase a bespoke Wool Press with accompanying Weigh Bar to improve the management and efficiency of packing and storing Dartmoor sheep's wool on farm.
The farm was already an established storage hub, but additional support would enable them to build on their existing operation.

FiPL recognised the need for a designated wool storage facility on Dartmoor. Greenwell Farm was approved for funding in 2025-26. They were awarded a grant of ~£25k for their wool press and improvements to their wool processing unit. Prior to receiving funding, they stored wool on site for over 50 local farms and processed up to 50 tonnes of wool each year. This funding enables Greenwell Farm to support more smaller local farms that often get overlooked. The project also helps to increase the resilience of their own farm by allowing them to continue diversifying.

The Greenwell Farm & Twool projects, although separate, are closely connected: one was helping to provide the local infrastructure needed to process wool and the other helping create more demand for the Dartmoor wool.

Dartmoor's historic wool industry no longer exists, but through this funding we’re reviving the trade, and use of this natural material. The projects strengthen the local supply chain, build resilience and create new opportunities for Dartmoor farmers to generate income from their Whiteface Dartmoor sheep's wool.
If we can continue to build a market for Dartmoor wool, then we will add value to it as a raw material.
FiPL funding future development
FiPL supports innovative, one-off projects that:

The Twool project is rooted on Dartmoor and the success of this project places Dartmoor, and our farmers, at the centre of it. The initial FiPL grant provided Twool with crucial seed funding and proof of concept. This funding acted as a stepping stone, enabling them to go on to be successful in applying for a more long-term grant through Innovate UK to support the project's future development. Through Innovate UK, Twool was awarded a grant of nearly £10k for wool rope trials in 2024-25.
This is exactly what FiPL likes to see: funding which will result in outcomes that serve as evidence to apply for additional funding support beyond FiPL.

The projects contribute to maintaining the distinctive character of Dartmoor’s landscape. Both projects strongly demonstrate the ‘Place’ FiPL programme theme – helping to increase in the resilience of nature friendly sustainable farm businesses across Dartmoor, helping to build a thriving local economy.
Supporting a local wool storage facility also develops a more localised wool supply chain, reduces transport miles, fuel consumption and greenhouse gas emissions.

While FiPL operates within a defined eligibility framework, its innovative and locally tailored nature allows flexibility. Our local FiPL team are vital in providing local, contextual advice to individual projects.

Together, these projects demonstrate the importance of locally delivered grant programmes. They work at the grassroots, with local farmers and local businesses to support innovative place-based outcomes that benefit the landscape.
FiPL has been absolutely delighted to support these two creative projects, and we look forward to hearing about their successes in the future.
