title: Beyond knowledge: what dairy farmers can teach us about behaviour change in antibiotic stewardship

content.content: This week is World Antimicrobial Resistance (AMR) Awareness Week and the perfect opportunity to hear from one of the scholars participating in the VMD-University of Zambia postgraduate programme, Inyambo Mumbula. Funded by the Fleming Fund and supported by technical expertise from VMD, his research focuses on antimicrobial resistance in Zambia, centred around smallholder dairy farmers. In this blog, Inyambo brings to life how his research has put farmers at the centre of improving antimicrobial stewardship.
What can a smallholder dairy farmer teach an environmental safety officer, a social policy expert or a digital health specialist about behaviour change?
More than we might expect.

Over the last three years, my research has explored the knowledge, attitudes and practices of smallholder dairy farmers in Zambia regarding the use of antimicrobials. Smallholder dairy farmers manage relatively small herds of non-native breeds such as Friesian or Jersey cows, or local breeds which produce low milk yields primarily for household consumption or local market sales.

My research identified gaps in knowledge and practices around the responsible use of antimicrobials, with potential implications for the development of AMR. In response, I employed a Social and Behaviour Change (SBC) approach to develop a radio- and text message-based intervention designed to reach smallholder farmers and support better antimicrobial stewardship.
Putting antibiotic stewardship on the airwaves

The resulting intervention used a radio drama, interactive radio discussions and text messages to communicate good antimicrobial stewardship practices in an accessible and locally relevant way. Rather than relying solely on technical information, the radio content placed decisions about antimicrobial use within situations farmers could recognise from everyday life. Text messages complemented the radio programmes by providing reminders and reinforcing important behaviours between episodes. The intervention was developed with farmers using Human-Centred Design, so their perspectives helped shape not only what was communicated, but how it was communicated.
Taking the lessons to UNICEF

On 11–12 June 2026, I joined a UNICEF learning event on Social and Behaviour Change, focused on how we can better listen to communities and co-design interventions with them. The diversity in the room included government ministries, United Nations agencies, civil society organisations, SBC practitioners and digital institutions working across health, water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH), social policy and community development. This diversity reinforced an important message: SBC is not confined to one sector or discipline.
During the meeting, I shared insights from my PhD research. Three lessons stood out:

One of the issues I explored was adherence to antimicrobial withdrawal periods. This is the length of time that must lapse between the final administration of the medicine and the point that the treated animal can be slaughtered to enter the food chain or when produce, such as milk, can be taken from the treated animal. Withdrawal periods exist to ensure the medicinal substances have been adequately metabolised or excreted. On paper, the solution can appear straightforward: educate farmers about withdrawal periods, explain the risks of antimicrobial residues in animal products, and reinforce the rules with regulatory actions and sanctions. But listening to farmers revealed a much more complex reality.

Some farmers knew about antimicrobial withdrawal periods yet chose not to comply with them. For instance, milk was sold through informal markets, processed or allowed to sour, while some believed that boiling could make the milk safe. These practices were often responses to livelihood pressures, household needs, market demands and limited access to veterinary support and advice, rather than necessarily evidence of ignorance or disregard for regulations.  This was an important reminder that knowledge alone may not be enough to support good practices and the threat of sanctions does not automatically produce sustained behaviour change. People make decisions within real-life circumstances. For SBC practitioners and those of us invested in promoting antimicrobial stewardship, this means that asking “What don’t people know?” may not be enough. We also need to ask: “What circumstances make this behaviour difficult, and what are people trying to achieve through it?”
A second lesson was about the role of radio and text messaging.

In an era where Mobile Health - the practice of medicine and public health supported by mobile and wireless devices - is often associated with sophisticated mobile applications, digital platforms and smartphones, it can be tempting to assume that newer technology automatically means better interventions.
My research suggested otherwise for many smallholder farmers in rural areas.

Radio remains an important and trusted source of information, particularly where internet connectivity, smartphone ownership and data affordability can limit access to digital platforms. The value of radio lay in its reliability, familiarity and local relevance. Using local announcers created an opportunity to communicate in familiar voices and languages and to connect messages to the community’s existing information networks. Radio also allowed the intervention to move beyond one-way messaging through interactive discussions and phone-in programmes.

Text messaging provided another layer of reinforcement. Rather than expecting farmers to remember everything from a single programme, text messages could reinforce key behaviours afterwards while reminding them about upcoming episodes.

The lesson for me was that “low-tech” should not be confused with “low-value.” The most appropriate technology is the one that fits people’s realities, routines and accesses and leverages trusted communication channels.  At the same time, this does not mean that radio and text messaging are the communication channels we need to use to reach everyone. Urban farmers and other populations with greater smartphone access may benefit from different Mobile Health approaches, including mobile applications, WhatsApp-based interventions, digital decision support tools, or more interactive platforms. The question should therefore not be “What technology is newest?” but “What technology fits the people, context and behaviour we are trying to influence?”

Perhaps the most important contribution of Human-Centred Design was that it helped me to move from focusing on which intervention I should deliver, to first understanding how the community wanted to be reached. Through co-design, farmers helped identify the importance of making the radio intervention engaging, familiar and locally relevant. This contributed to the decision to use a drama series, supported by text messages and locally familiar forms of storytelling and engagement, including kuyabila - a traditional poetic chanting or poetry used for local engagement and storytelling.

The drama format created an opportunity to place antimicrobial stewardship within everyday situations rather than presenting it only as technical information. Farmers could encounter characters, dilemmas and consequences that reflected experiences familiar to their own lives.

The use of kuyabila similarly provided an opportunity to draw on a locally meaningful form of expression and engagement, making the intervention feel less like an externally imposed health message and more connected to the community’s own ways of communicating.

Perhaps the most rewarding part of sharing this One Health experience at the UNICEF event was seeing how readily the lessons resonated with people working far beyond antimicrobial stewardship and outside animal health.

Lessons from dairy farmers can inform other sectors. The sectors may differ, but the behavioural questions remain similar: Have we listened? Do we understand the context? And have communities had a meaningful role in shaping the solution?
When we listen first, lessons travel far – and we design better.

title: Choosing a new management information system (MIS) - here's what you need to know before you buy
authors: Emma Bagley, MIS Commercial Lead, Department for Education

content.content: A new Department for Education (DfE) framework for buying a cloud-based management information system (MIS) is launching in September 2027. Ahead of this, there are steps you should take now depending on when your current contract ends.
This is a summary of the key actions that will help you stay compliant and avoid being locked into arrangements that delay your move to the new framework:
If your contracts expire shortly after launch, check whether there is enough time to use the framework and, if changing systems, complete the transition safely.
Why this matters to trusts now

The department is working towards the provision of a new MIS framework, due to be available in September 2027. The framework is designed not only to support compliance, but also to provide schools and trusts with greater transparency over costs, fairer contractual arrangements, clearer routes for resolving disputes, and improved protection from supplier lock-in.

Once it's live, you will be expected to use it for MIS procurement, rather than procuring directly from suppliers or via an alternative framework. This is to ensure that you benefit from the sector-specific terms and conditions.

The framework has been developed through extensive engagement with schools, trusts and suppliers since late 2025, including a sector working group established in February 2026. Feedback continues to shape the final framework requirements.

The framework is also designed to support a healthy and competitive market. It will reopen annually, allowing new suppliers to apply and existing suppliers to refresh their offers. This means schools and trusts will continue to benefit from innovation and choice, while gaining stronger contractual protections.

From 1 October 2026, the Academy Trust Handbook (para 2.30) states that trusts must ensure that all MIS contracts are aligned with DfE’s MIS framework by September 2027. More details about your contract management are available in the section below.

Where an existing MIS contract extends past September 2027, trusts are able to continue with that contract until it expires but should not exercise any available extension options. This ensures trusts benefit from the added protections offered by the framework.

If a trust does not comply, it will need to be able to explain why, for example insufficient network connectivity to host a cloud solution. Achieving better commercial rates will not be a valid exemption, as the framework is designed to deliver a wider range of benefits rather than be limited to cost savings. There is no reason why a supplier should charge you more for supplying via the DfE framework when compared to another route.
Why this matters to local authority-maintained schools

Local-authority-maintained schools are still expected to use the framework and follow the guidance in order to access the same value-for-money and protections that trusts will benefit from. However, as local authority-maintained schools are not covered by the Academy Trust Handbook, it is not a mandatory requirement for you.
Using the framework will also be in line with the communication issued on 8 June 2026 by the then Secretary of State for Education, Bridget Phillipson.
What you need to do with your existing MIS contract

Check when your current MIS contract ends, and act accordingly. If you have already started a compliant procurement exercise, you do not need to stop or restart it because of the forthcoming framework. If you're unsure, contact the department for advice or review one of the "Power Hour" recordings.

Scenario A: If your contract expires before 1 September 2027, extend it or replace it for a maximum of 12 months. Treat this as a transitional arrangement, bridging the gap until you can procure through the DfE framework.

Scenario B: If your supplier won't offer a 12-month extension, you'll need to re-procure instead. In this case, avoid signing a contract that runs for more than 3 years, including any extensions, so you're able to move to the DfE framework at your next renewal point. You should also look to seek agreement from the supplier and/or include in your procurement and contract documents the Core Principles, covered in section 3.

Scenario C: If your contract runs beyond 1 September 2027, don't use extension options that would delay your transition to the framework. When an academy trust awards its next full-term MIS contract, you must use the DfE MIS framework.

Scenario D: Your setting does not have sufficient network connectivity to host a cloud-based MIS and therefore needs to procure a MIS hosted by an ‘on-premises’ server. In this scenario, it is still advised that you seek the supplier’s agreement to the Core Principles (covered in section 3), and/or include them in your procurement and contract documents.
The Core Principles for interim procurement
If you fall into Scenario A, B or D above, and need to run any procurement activity before the framework launches, you should build specific safeguards into your tender documents.

Until the DfE framework launches, some schools and trusts will still need to procure or extend an MIS contract. If this applies to you, the guidance requires you to build the Core Principles into your tender documents and obtain supplier confirmation in writing.
Ask every potential supplier to do three things to avoid confusion later:
Speak to your data protection officer as part of this process since data protection is a key part of any MIS decision. The procuring EdTech guidance has more detail.
Staying on track and getting help
This is a multi-year transition with a national deadline.

Between now and launch, we'll keep engaging with schools, trusts and suppliers through webinars, sector events and published guidance. The questions you raise through these channels will directly shape our supporting materials and frequently asked questions (FAQs) ahead of implementation.
Expect regular updates as we move towards the September 2027 launch, including FAQs, practical guidance, "Power Hours", and answers to the questions schools and trusts are asking us.

title: New funding for peatland restoration in England

content.content: Last month the government announced a new £25 million Peatland Restoration Grant Scheme. This blog post provides more detail.
Over two years, the scheme will help local partnerships, environmental organisations and land managers restore degraded peatlands across England.

This funding will help maintain the skills, partnerships and momentum that have developed across the peatland restoration sector from earlier schemes such as the Nature for Climate Peatland Grant Scheme.
It will help support the government’s goals on climate and nature recovery, while building stronger resilience to wildfire in peatland landscapes.

The funding will be available for peatlands across the country. It will sit alongside other funding for lowland agricultural peat, which is focused on improving water management and developing wetter farming approaches.
Why restore peatlands?
Healthy peatlands are valuable for nature, climate and communities. They store vast amounts of carbon, and support rare and important plants and animals.

But when peatlands become dry and degraded, they cannot provide these benefits. Dry peatlands can also be particularly susceptible to wildfire, which damages habitats, releases carbon and creates long-lasting impacts for nearby communities and land managers.
How can we restore them?
We restore peatlands by getting them wet again. This can mean blocking drainage ditches, reshaping the land to hold more water, and bringing back bog-building plants like sphagnum moss.
Taking action on peatlands protects the carbon stored in them, improves habitat condition and helps landscapes cope with a changing climate – including wildfire.
Because of the increased risk of wildfire, the new scheme will particularly welcome projects that deliver increased wildfire resilience.
Bringing more investment into peatland restoration
Public funding, such as this new scheme, will continue to play an important role in restoring peatlands, but will not be enough on its own to achieve our ambitions for nature recovery.

We want more businesses to support credible peatland projects and participate responsibly in nature markets. Private investment can play an important role in complementing public funding, bringing in additional resources of restoration.

The new scheme will place a stronger emphasis on projects that can secure suitable match funding, or explore where responsible blended finance could help restoration go further. It will also support projects to develop their financial plans and, where appropriate, be in a better position to attract private investment in the future.

Where projects participate in nature markets, mechanisms such as the Peatland Code, or schemes aligned with the BSI Nature Investment Standards, can help provide market confidence in the environmental outcomes being delivered.
Building the pipeline and supporting ongoing management
The scheme will also offer discovery funding to help projects do the early work needed to turn an idea into a deliverable restoration project.
This could be support in preparing restoration and financial plans, carrying out surveys and involving the people and organisations that need to be part of the work.

Natural England and Defra are working to ensure sites that are restored through the scheme can easily access ongoing land management payments through Countryside Stewardship Higher Tier, rewarding land managers for restoring their peatlands.
Developing the peatland restoration sector

Alongside funding restoration works, we are investing in the people, skills and equipment needed to grow England's peatland restoration sector through the Peatland Restoration Sector Capacity Grant Scheme.

This year, the scheme is supporting a range of projects across England, from specialist machinery, including an all-terrain vehicle in Cumbria and a monitoring drone in Cheshire, to additional apprentices and interns in Derbyshire and Sheffield, and staff training and upskilling in Devon and within the National Trust.
Running annually until 2030, the scheme will complement wider restoration funding by helping the sector build and sustain the capacity needed for long-term delivery.
What happens next?

Natural England will deliver the Peatland Restoration Grant Scheme. It will publish further information about how the scheme will work and what applicants will need to provide later this month. Applications are expected to open in early 2027, with grant awards starting in spring 2027.

Existing Nature for Climate Peatland Grant Scheme grant recipients will need to apply to the new scheme. Applications will also be welcomed from organisations and partnerships that have not previously received peat restoration funding.

This new funding will maintain momentum in peatland restoration, delivering our Environmental Improvement Plan and Net Zero targets, whilst building resilience to wildfire and strengthening the partnerships needed to deliver work on the ground.

title: Introducing our new report: Landscape, species and anthropogenic change 5: Ancient grasslands

content.content: By Hannah Rigden, Senior Historic Environment Officer, Landscape, Heritage and Geodiversity Team

This blog introduces a new Natural England report, Landscape, species and anthropogenic change 5: Ancient grasslands, the first in a series. The report reviews the archaeological, historical and palaeoecological literature to bring together the most up-to-date evidence on who shaped England's habitats, what changed, why, when and how.

The series also offers an introduction to the clues about past land use that you can find in place names, field patterns and buildings. Illustrated timelines show the trends in how habitats formed and were lost over time.
Our evidence helps us to:
Over my career, I have had some amazing places as "my patch". These experiences have shaped my own connection to nature and how I work. Let me tell you about one of my favourite pieces of casework.
Rose End Meadows

I was at Rose End Meadows SSSI, meeting one of the farmers to talk about how he managed his land. Sweet cicely in the verges smelled of aniseed. I was surrounded by tiny, irregularly shaped fields, many smaller than a tennis court. Each field seemed to have its own community of plants, with different colours and textures. It was very peaceful.

One field had an uneven surface, rocky, sloping and patchy. There were hay meadow flowers such as yellow rattle, orchids, knapweed and meadow vetchling, alongside patches of hawthorn scrub, taller grass with few flowers, and bare ground. The farmer told me the land had been in his family for many years and had always been tricky to farm, but that he loved this place.

These fields had not always been so green. The hollows and stony bare patches were the remains of many long-abandoned lead mines, and some fields also had medieval ridge and furrow. Only heavy-metal-tolerant lichens and spring sandwort (locally known as leadwort) grew in the stones. The collapsing mines and small fields made using machinery difficult, and the lead in the soil was poisonous to livestock.
Where fields could not be grazed or mown, the bushes had grown, the grasses had become tall, and the vegetation community had changed from what it was when the SSSI was first designated.

My task, and one I loved, was to work with the farmer to balance his needs with those of Natural England. We needed to keep his cattle healthy and the farm viable, while honouring his deep roots in the area. At the same time, I had to consider whether he was meeting the terms of his agri-environment agreement to look after the nature, heritage and landscape, and whether the SSSI was moving towards favourable condition.

I couldn't solve everything in one visit. We needed to do something about the scrub and find a way to take a hay cut. But I learned a lot about the area, and I saw that one management method can never fit every situation, not even every field on the same farm.

A couple of years later, I went back. A contractor had cut and treated the scrub, and had borrowed small hand-propelled machinery to cut as much of the grass as they could. I was able to say that this part of the SSSI was now in recovering condition. Most rewarding of all, the farmer told me that the skylarks he remembered from his childhood were nesting here again after many years, and he was proud of what he had achieved.

By trying to understand the industrial and family history of the farm, and the need for bespoke decisions for each field, I was able to negotiate a good outcome. Taking an integrated approach to managing the land at Rose End aimed at keeping the character of the landscape and help the farmer stay connected to his land, while making a start on recovering the diversity of its wildlife.

We do not know what choices we will have to make in future as the climate changes and land changes hands. But by using evidence from our deep past, we will be able to see how habitats react to new conditions and make better-informed decisions.

title: From flood risk to action: helping people take the next step

content.content: Understanding your flood risk is important. But understanding something does not necessarily mean you will act on it.
Over the past year, the Check your long term flood risk team has been exploring what helps people move from understanding their flood risk to taking practical steps to prepare.
Our starting point was simple: how might we help someone take one useful next step, without overwhelming them with information?
Understanding risk does not always lead to action
Our earlier discovery work suggested a lack of information was not always the problem.

People can understand flooding is a risk but still be unsure what they should do, where to start, or whether acting now is reasonable. That led us to a simple proposition: help people move one step closer to resilience by making actions clear, manageable and relevant to their circumstances.
We wanted to understand that problem better before changing the service.

Our research combined surveys with 927 people and face-to-face workshops with 35 people in Mablethorpe and Gloucester, including people who are digitally disadvantaged. The surveys showed us broader patterns, while the workshops helped us understand the barriers behind them.
People want to prepare, but taking the first step can be difficult
The survey gave us an encouraging picture.
63.4% of respondents said preparing in advance was important, but 17% intended to prepare and had not yet acted.
That suggested an opportunity for the service. We did not necessarily need to persuade everyone flooding mattered. For some people, we needed to make the first step easier and clearer.

To understand what might help people take a first step, we asked which information and actions mattered most. Flood warnings were the top priority, chosen by 53.4%, followed by understanding local flood risk (45.5%) and what was being done to protect their area (44.4%).
But the open comments revealed a broader picture. People also talked about stress, isolation and financial concerns, including insurance, affordability and recovery.
For us, it was an important reminder: what people select in a survey does not always capture what matters when they have space to describe their experience.
The same action is not equally easy for everyone
Our workshops helped us explore these experiences in more depth.

They showed the same recommendation can be straightforward for one household and difficult for another. Familiar, free actions such as signing up for flood warnings felt more achievable, while cost, lack of awareness and the need for specialist support could create barriers to other actions.
We also heard about the importance of accessible and non-digital routes, trusted community networks and clearer information about who is responsible for what locally.
These findings suggested simply presenting people with a longer list of things they could do would not necessarily help.
Making the next step clearer
Rather than redesigning the whole journey at once, we identified a small change we could test. We made our existing actions easier to act on directly from someone's flood-risk result.

Previously, the route into an action could be easy to overlook because it competed with other content on the page. We changed the hierarchy so people now see their flood-risk level followed immediately by a recommended action. Depending on the information available for their location, that might be getting free flood warnings or finding out how to prepare for flooding on GOV.UK. If the available risk information does not justify recommending an action, we do not push one.
It was a deliberately focused intervention: put the risk and a proportionate next step together, rather than adding more information.
Measuring whether the change made a difference
We released the first-phase change in October to coincide with Flood Action Week and began measuring how people interacted with it.

The early results are encouraging. Among people checking an address where they or someone they know lives, click-through to an action increased from around 6% to 22%. We saw increases among other user groups too.
Those are useful signals, but they are not proof that making an action more prominent makes people more resilient.
A click is not the same as being better prepared. We still need to understand what people do next and whether other factors contributed to the increase.
Small changes can help us learn quickly

This work has reinforced that user-centred design does not always mean making a large change. By combining research with behavioural data from the live service, we identified a point of friction and made a small, measurable intervention.
Our next step is to understand why some people do not engage with the recommended action.
Ultimately, we want to make it easier for people to understand what their flood risk means for them and take a useful next step.
Natalie Smithson is a senior content designer at Defra.

title: How a library book inspired my career in antimicrobial resistance (AMR)

content.content: I have always had a passion for reading, and anything science-based with a bit of ‘make believe’ captivated me. So, when I picked up a book from the school library titled ‘Plague’ by Malcolm Rose, I knew I was going to enjoy the book, however, I did not realise it would influence my future career!

The book follows a modern-day plague sweeping through England with scientists racing to find the cure. Factual sections on disease, viruses, human and animal infections and routes of transmission, sprinkled into a couple of teenagers trying to find the cure, and I was hooked. From that moment, my fascination began. I read everything I could on viral and bacterial infections, fiction and non-fiction, I even subjected my friends and family to presentations on all I had learnt!

As my interest grew, I went to study Human Biosciences at university where I began to appreciate the growing challenge of antimicrobial resistance (AMR). During my studies, I undertook a dissertation in AMR, understanding resistance mechanisms and routes of transmission. From there, I completed a PhD in biodiscovery, trying to source new antimicrobials to treat AMR infections and that brings me to where I am today…
My role at APHA

Working at APHA in the UK Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) Reference Centre for AMR has been an incredibly rewarding experience. It has allowed me to share my knowledge, connect with like-minded colleagues, and develop a greater appreciation of the complex global challenges associated with AMR. Building collaborations with partners across the UK and West Africa is a central part of my role. No two days are the same, but they often involve engaging with international colleagues, supporting capacity-strengthening activities, discussing surveillance approaches, and exploring new opportunities for research and innovation.

One of the aspects I enjoy most is the opportunity to share knowledge and learn from others, whether that is in the sense of AMR, culture or alternative approaches to tackling complex issues. AMR affects countries in different ways, and there is a tremendous amount we can gain through collaboration and exchanging expertise. Africa and Asia are regions where AMR is predicted to hit the hardest, so why not collaborate and learn from each other? We offer guidance and support from policy to implementation and data analysis, where they educate us on the unique challenges faced in-country for surveillance, diagnostics, and antimicrobial stewardship, together we can find appropriate solutions.
What has surprised me most working in AMR?

I always used to view AMR as largely a scientific based problem, with a laboratory-based solution. However, AMR is much more complex, and whilst the science is fundamental, AMR is much larger than that. I have come to appreciate that it is also societal, economic, environmental and a political challenge.

During my time at the Welsh Government, AMR was always referred to as a ‘wicked problem’, a challenge with many interrelated biological and social drivers, where action is required in a multitude of ways. Perhaps, most importantly, I have learned just how global this issue is. Resistant organisms can emerge in one location and quickly become a concern elsewhere. No single organisation, country or sector can tackle AMR alone. Success depends on strong partnerships and a willingness to work together toward a shared goal.
The familiar term ‘One Health’

Throughout this blog, I have highlighted the importance of collaboration as a way of developing solutions to AMR. One Health is the very same, this term highlights the importance of addressing AMR across human, animal, plant and environment sectors, because AMR is transboundary and cross-sectoral. The UK FAO Reference Centre encompasses organisations and experts across these sectors; APHAprotects animal and plant health with a specialism in AMR in farmed animals, their environment and food; marine and freshwater science experts at the Centre for Environment, Fisheries and Aquaculture Science have a specialism in AMR in aquatic animals and the environment; whilst the Veterinary Medicines Directorateare the UK competent authority for veterinary medicines, responsible for AMR and residues policy for animals. Together, we can coordinate our expertise and deliver programs of work in a One Health manner with overseas partners.
A look to the future

The future of AMR research is both challenging and exciting. Advances in genomics, diagnostics, surveillance technologies and antimicrobial discovery are providing new opportunities to better understand and respond to resistance. However, scientific advances alone will not solve the problem. Raising awareness remains critically important. Everyone has a role to play, whether through responsible antimicrobial use, supporting infection prevention measures or simply understanding why AMR matters.
I hope to continue contributing to the global effort against AMR by strengthening collaborations, supporting capacity building and helping translate scientific knowledge into practical action.

Looking back, it is remarkable to think that a book borrowed from a school library helped set me on this path. What began as curiosity about a fictional outbreak has grown into a career dedicated to understanding and addressing one of the biggest health challenges of our time.

This World Antimicrobial Awareness Week is an opportunity to reflect on how far we have come, but also on how much work remains ahead. Through collaboration, innovation and a shared commitment to One Health, we can help preserve the effectiveness of antimicrobials for future generations.

title: Eyes on Waste Crime: why your call matters

content.content: How to do the right thing with your waste

You've probably seen it. The lorry turning up at odd hours. The site that's suddenly full when it was empty last month. The smoke that shouldn't be there, or the smell that lingers too long. You know your community. You know when something's wrong.
That instinct is good. Trust it.
Today we're launching Eyes on Waste Crime, asking people across Kent to report what they see. Because waste crime isn't a minor offence. It's organised crime, and it thrives in silence.
Why we're asking you to look, and to call

Waste crime takes many shapes, from illegal dumping on a quiet lane to gangs filling warehouses with thousands of tonnes of waste. Whatever the scale, it harms the places where people live, the land farmers depend on, and the businesses trying to do things properly. It costs the economy over £1 billion a year. But that figure doesn't capture the smell, the blight, or the fear that stops a neighbour picking up the phone.

In Kent, we know this is happening. We also know many residents have seen it without reporting it, not because they don't care, but because they're not sure who to call, don't believe anything will change, or worry about being identified. We're here to change that.
You don't need proof. You don't need your name.

If something looks wrong, lorries at odd hours, waste piling up where it wasn't before, smoke or water pollution, trust your instinct and call us. You don't need evidence and you don't need to give your name. Your identity stays protected.
Your call leads to real action

We act on what you tell us. We've shut down illegal sites, suspended and revoked permits, and secured prosecutions, because people reported what they saw. Every report adds to the picture. Every report counts.
How to report suspected waste crime
Seen illegal dumping, suspicious waste movements or burning, an unlicensed operator, or a disposal offer that seems too cheap to be legal? Call our waste hotline on 0800 80 70 60, any hour, any day.
Doing the right thing with your own waste
Most people want to dispose of their waste properly. Here's how to make sure you do, and how to avoid helping a criminal without realising it.

Before you pay anyone to take your waste away, check the Environment Agency public register of waste carriers. If they're not on it, they're breaking the law, and you could be held responsible if your waste ends up dumped illegally. Ask where it's going and keep a written record.

If you own land, check it regularly, even if it's empty. Secure it with barriers or concrete blocks and consider CCTV. You can be held liable for waste dumped on your land, even if you didn't put it there. Find out more: Property and Landowners – how to avoid waste criminals – Environment Agency: For homes and habitats.

For everyday household waste and recycling, your local council is still your first port of call, including for bulky waste collection and your nearest recycling centre. Find out more: Dispose of household waste - GOV.UK
Report it. Every time.
Keep an eye on waste crime. If you see it, or suspect it, call 0800 80 70 60. Every report helps us protect your community, your environment, and the honest businesses doing this the right way.
With your help, we can tackle waste crime and protect homes and habitats for generations to come.
